title: A systematic framework for the design, simulation and optimization of personalized healthcare: making and healing blood
contribution: Consortium review of an in vitro / in silico / in vivo framework for biomedical systems, with Misener's bioreactor superstructure MINLP (solved by ANTIGONE, with robust optimisation) as the type 1 example and leukaemia chemotherapy as the type 2 example.
problem_entry: Personalised medicine needs validated in vitro systems and predictive models (p. 3); ex vivo blood costs $8330/unit vs $225.42 for a transfused unit, so optimisation enters through cost (p. 5).
key_idea: Bioreactor design and operation as a superstructure MINLP minimising the cost of one RBC unit, implemented in GAMS and solved with ANTIGONE 1.1 (p. 7); formulation with integer fibre counts in Appendix 1 (pp. 28-31).
assumptions: Uncertain parameters listed with ranges (p. 30); sensitivity analysis picks the influential ones, cellular flux across ceramic fibres first (p. 28); robust optimisation over worst-case realisations (p. 7).
proof_devices: sensitivity analysis -> robust optimisation -> repeated runs over scenarios (p. 7)
split of design decisions into invariant (long, thin, many fibres, high flow) and sensitive (minimum polymeric fibres) (p. 8)
experiments: none of its own for the optimisation part; cites Misener et al. 2014b for cost competitiveness (p. 7)
positioning: Presents the BSEL/CPSE framework and cites prior consortium papers (Misener et al. 2014a,b; Pefani et al.; Fuentes-Garí et al.) as building blocks (pp. 7-11).
writing: Framework figure plus two worked domains; full optimisation model relegated to an appendix (pp. 4-5, 28-31).
limits_future: Generic future work on grey/white-box models from biomarkers (p. 14); on-line optimisation and control for anaesthesia 'remains to be addressed' (p. 13).

method_links.note: The partner's mechanistic bioreactor model (not a trained ML model) written as a MINLP and solved globally with her own ANTIGONE; design rules returned to experimentalists.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: After robust optimisation, design choices invariant to parameter/model changes are listed with physical reasons, separately from the sensitive fibre-count trade-off.

transferable: Report design decisions under uncertainty as two lists: invariant ones with their physical cause, and sensitive ones with the trade-off that moves them (p. 8).
Put the full optimisation model (objective, constraints, uncertain-parameter table, variable bounds) in an appendix of a framework paper (pp. 28-31).
coauthors: M. Fuentes-Garí, E. Velliou, E. Pefani, M. Rende, N. Panoskaltsis, A. Mantalaris, E. N. Pistikopoulos (corresponding)

quotes.text: The model is implemented in GAMS 24.1 and solved using the MINLP solver ANTIGONE 1.1 (Misener and Floudas, 2013; 2014).
Robust optimization helps quantify these tradeoffs (Appendix 1).

title: A mathematical model of subpopulation kinetics for the deconvolution of leukaemia heterogeneity
contribution: A cyclin/DNA-based population balance model of the leukaemia cell cycle, validated on three cell lines and in blinded co-culture experiments that predict and deconvolute heterogeneous populations.
problem_entry: Existing cell-cycle PBMs use unmeasurable (age) or noisy (size) state variables and cannot inform experiments (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Measurable state variables per phase (cyclin E, DNA, cyclin B), upwind discretisation into ODEs, comparison with flow-cytometry geometric means (pp. 4-7).
assumptions: Aggregated G0/G1 and G2/M phases (p. 5); normal-CDF transition probabilities (p. 5); maximum cyclin at 99.99% transition (p. 7).
proof_devices: numerical cell-conservation test with duplication factor 1 (p. 7)
Sobol GSA on 24 parameters to decide what must be measured (pp. 8-9, 12)
experiments: EdU chase experiments on K-562, MEC-1, MOLT-4; co-culture fit/validation; nine blinded mixtures with forward/backward prediction and scenario ranking, misses reported (pp. 9-10).
positioning: Positions against age-, size- and DNA-based PBMs and single-cell models (pp. 3-4).
writing: Contributions statement assigns roles by initials; limits explained concretely at the points of mismatch (pp. 9-10, 15).
limits_future: No nutrient depletion in the model; cell-line density limits; close cycle times of the cell lines vs primary cells; future PK/PD coupling (pp. 10-12).

method_links.note: Weak: failures of the blinded tests written in (T4, T5; 2 of 3 backward predictions), but model-vs-experiment rather than solver comparison.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Operator 1 prepares unknown mixtures, blinded operator 2 runs the model, panel revealed and ranked, misses listed; idea credited to A. Mantalaris in the contributions statement, so consortium practice rather than Misener's own.

transferable: Run GSA before experiment design to decide which parameters must be measured and which can stay nominal (pp. 8-9).
Validate a predictive model with a blinded two-operator protocol and count the failures (pp. 9-10).
Choose measurable state variables so the model aggregates to the instrument's own statistic (pp. 4, 7).
coauthors: M. Fuentes-Garí, D. García-Münzer, E. Velliou, M. C. Georgiadis, M. Kostoglou, E. N. Pistikopoulos, N. Panoskaltsis, A. Mantalaris (corresponding)

quotes.text: Operator 2, blinded to the nature of the samples, performed the analysis at time 0 and determined the initial percent of each cell type in order to run the model.
RM carried out the experiments and participated in the model development, as well as providing feedback throughout.

title: Selecting a differential equation cell cycle model for simulating leukemia treatment
contribution: Compares ODE, a new DDE and a PBM cell-cycle model by fit, degrees of freedom and parameter measurability, and shows inside a common PK/PD chemotherapy model that the choice of cell-cycle model changes predicted treatment outcome.
problem_entry: GSA of an existing PK/PD model showed phase durations dominate; hypothesis that the cell-cycle model itself, not only its parameters, changes simulated response (p. 4).
key_idea: Judge three model classes both on chemotherapy-free fit and when embedded in the same PK/PD model, after converting parameters to a common steady state (pp. 4-5, 23-24).
assumptions: DDE not closed, transient total-cell variation < 3% (p. 7); oscillation tolerance 1% set by experimental error (p. 18); three degrees of freedom per phase needed for oscillations (pp. 18-19).
proof_devices: degree-of-freedom counting against observable oscillation features (pp. 18-19, 23)
linear stability analysis of the ODE model (p. 15)
Sobol GSA short-term and over 500 h (pp. 14, 19-20)
parameter conversion equalising growth rate and steady-state fractions across models (pp. 23-24, Table 4)
experiments: Fits on three cell lines (Tables 2-3, pp. 16-17); one example patient under a standard Ara-C/DNR protocol simulated with all three models (pp. 25-26).
positioning: Extends Pefani et al.'s CCP-ODE and Fuentes-Garí et al.'s CCP-PBM; new DDE contrasted with Colijn-Mackey DDEs whose parameters are hard to measure (p. 4).
writing: Results organised as questions ('Can the models fit experimental data?', 'Can the necessary parameters be measured?') (pp. 14-20).
limits_future: Concedes the DDE could gain from phase-duration variability at one extra parameter per phase (pp. 26, 28); selection criteria for chemotherapy-optimisation models listed (p. 29).

method_links.note: Component (cell-cycle model) judged inside the full PK/PD treatment model; isolated fit (DDE ~ PBM) differs from the in-system verdict.
Models put on equal footing (same steady state) before comparison, analogue of harmonised settings; rival improvement conceded.

transferable: Before comparing model classes inside a larger system, convert parameters so all share the same steady state, then compare dynamics under the intervention (pp. 23-24).
Count each model's degrees of freedom against the observable features it must match before fitting (pp. 18-19).
Set numerical tolerances from the experimental error (p. 18).
coauthors: M. Fuentes-Garí, M. C. Georgiadis, M. Kostoglou, N. Panoskaltsis, A. Mantalaris, E. N. Pistikopoulos

quotes.text: Based on this choice, and for CCP-PBM/CCP-DDE/CCP-ODE comparisons to be fair, the total kinetics (so that the cell number is equal) and the cell cycle distribution (so that the percentage of cells likely to be affected when chemotherapy starts) will have to be equal at steady state.
Cell cycle model selection has a critical impact on predicted chemotherapy response.

title: Development of a hematopoietic microenvironment for the production of red blood cells (RBCs) in a novel 3D hollow fibre bioreactor
contribution: Meeting abstract characterising cell types and their spatial distribution in a 3D hollow-fibre bioreactor for ex vivo RBC production.
problem_entry: Ex vivo RBC production in suspension culture is costly and inefficient (p. 1).
key_idea: Characterise the bioreactor microenvironment by marker and distance from the hollow fibres (p. 1).
proof_devices: spatial statistics of marker-positive cells: distance bands from fibres and nearest-neighbour clustering (p. 1)
experiments: 28-day culture; flow cytometry, confocal and electron microscopy; 8-fold expansion by day 21 (p. 1).
positioning: Extends the group's earlier hollow-fibre bioreactor studies (p. 1).
limits_future: No limits stated; suggests cost-effective RBC production (p. 1).
coauthors: M. C. Allenby, A. Tahlawi, S. B. Dos Santos, Y. Hwang, N. Panoskaltsis, A. Mantalaris

quotes.text: The data suggest that the 3D hollow-fibre bioreactor spontaneously sustained a multilineage microenvironment, the understanding of which could facilitate the cost-effective production of functional RBCs.

title: Bayesian optimization with dimension scheduling: Application to biological systems
contribution: Dimension Scheduling Algorithm: BO that optimises over a sampled small subset of coordinates per iteration with per-subset GPs, cutting computation to about a fifth and usually finding lower objectives on microalgae parameter estimation (read as arXiv v1).
problem_entry: Broken assumption: BO presumes expensive experiments and cheap BO, but the microalgae simulation runs in a fraction of a second, so GP cost dominates; deterministic global optimisation is out of range at this size (arXiv pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Sample coordinate subsets from PCA-based importance, optimise EI over that subset with its own GP while clamping others at the incumbent; drops additive BO's disjoint-decomposition assumption (arXiv pp. 3-4).
assumptions: GP with squared-exponential kernel, EI optimised by DIRECT; weighted least-squares objective with weights equal to measurement-type means (arXiv pp. 3-4).
experiments: 10 model variants (d = 10-12) x 4 runs x 500 iterations vs standard BO, same initial data; subset size 2 chosen on M19; DSA not uniformly better (Table 1); ~1/5 computation time (arXiv pp. 4-5).
positioning: Closest to Kandasamy et al.'s additive BO, dismissed for this problem without numbers; deterministic global parameter estimation (Michalik et al.) cited as out of range (arXiv pp. 2-3).
writing: Three numbered benefits in the abstract; text refers to a nonexistent 'Figure 4' (arXiv p. 5).
limits_future: No global convergence guarantee; GP accuracy falls with d; pruning GPs by marginal likelihood and parallelisation proposed (arXiv pp. 6-7).

method_links.note: Subset-size parameter chosen on one model and fixed across all ten variants (no re-tuning), but robustness across the class not shown.
Losses kept in Table 1 and 'not uniformly superior' stated; but additive-BO rival dismissed without data.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: scope statement against her own core tool
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: States deterministic global optimisation is out of range for this problem size and chooses BO for its sensitivity information (cf. Heuristic 7, Workflow A checkpoint).

transferable: Enter a method paper through the inverted cost assumption (cheap evaluations, expensive optimiser) and redesign for that regime (arXiv pp. 1-2).
Keep losses in the results table and say in words that the method is not uniformly better (arXiv pp. 4-5).
State the guarantee lost next to the speed-up gained (arXiv p. 6).
coauthors: D. Ulmasov, C. Baroukh, B. Chachuat, M. P. Deisenroth (co-corresponding)

quotes.text: Problems of this size are, practically speaking, out of the range of current deterministic global optimization technology, so we are left to consider heuristics and gradient-based approaches.
Since the DSA algorithm never uses all of the data, we cannot assert global algorithm convergence.

title: A personalized framework for dynamic modeling of disease trajectories in chronic lymphocytic leukemia
contribution: A multi-compartment delay-differential model of CLL linking bone marrow, blood and lymph nodes/spleen by migration, with parameters calculated by a GAMS feasibility problem, applied to five hypothetical patients and analysed by global sensitivity analysis.
problem_entry: CLL spreads over four compartments with heterogeneous presentation; prior models are one- or two-compartment (pp. 1, 5-7).
key_idea: Three linked Mackey G0 DDE models with migration and bone-marrow carrying capacity; parameters split into assumed, measured (routine clinical tests) and calculated (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: 6 differential + 23 algebraic equations, 76 parameters (p. 3); assumptions (a)-(f) on normal lymphocytes, blood volume, recruitment rate, stage durations (p. 4); 90% of lymphocytes in affected tissue are CLL (p. 7).
proof_devices: GAMS feasibility problem seeded with initial/final cell numbers plus rule-based adjustment loop with error tolerances (p. 12)
multistart of the feasibility problem: 50 starts, trajectories within 10% (pp. 16-17)
experiments: Five hypothetical patients P1-P5 across Binet stage transitions; no real patient data; 0.1-0.2 CPU s per simulation (pp. 4-7).
positioning: Complements the one-compartment model of Nanda et al. and the two-compartment ibrutinib model; claims the first physiologically-relevant multi-compartment CLL model (pp. 1, 5-7).
writing: Numbered features of novelty in the introduction and conclusion; explicit 'reasonable rather than optimal' framing (pp. 1, 3, 7).
limits_future: Hypothetical cases only, validation with patient data needed; Binet C approximated; no convergence proof; migration and proliferation induction proposed as new clinical parameters (pp. 5, 7, 16).

method_links.note: Weak: non-uniqueness of the feasibility problem tested by multistart and reported in an appendix rather than hidden.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Parameter calculation posed as a feasibility problem, labelled as seeking reasonable rather than optimal parameters, with a multistart check of how much trajectories move (cf. Heuristic 4).

transferable: When data cannot identify parameters, solve a feasibility problem, call the result reasonable rather than optimal, and multistart it to bound the effect on conclusions (pp. 3, 12, 16).
Tabulate every parameter as assumed, measured (with the clinical test) or calculated (p. 3).
Use global sensitivity analysis to propose which unmeasured quantities should become clinical measurements (p. 5).
coauthors: S. Savvopoulos, N. Panoskaltsis, E. N. Pistikopoulos, A. Mantalaris

quotes.text: We seek reasonable parameters rather than guaranteed parameter estimates of the best possible values; our purpose is to capture disease dynamics.

We cannot prove that the algorithm will always converge to the same point, but this section demonstrates our computational experience that results of the Appendix D algorithm give answers within 10% of one another.

title: Spatiotemporal mapping of erythroid, stromal, and osteogenic niche formation to support physiologic red cell production in a three-dimensional hollow fibre perfusion bioreactor
contribution: ASH meeting abstract reporting long-term RBC production at 5-fold lower cytokine levels in a 3D hollow-fibre bioreactor, with niches mapped in space and time by the group's confocal image analysis.
problem_entry: In vitro erythroid cultures need unphysiologically high cytokines and low densities that exhaust progenitors (p. 1).
key_idea: Run the bioreactor with lower cytokine gradients and map cell clusters relative to the hollow fibres over time (p. 1).
proof_devices: confocal computational analysis of clusters and distance bands, method not described here (p. 1)
experiments: 28-day culture; >10^7 enucleated cells harvested; 23 cytokines measured; clusters 50-500 um with 10-20-fold local density (p. 1).
positioning: Extends the group's earlier HFBR reports (p. 1).
limits_future: No limits stated; platform for translational expansion protocols (p. 1).
coauthors: M. C. Allenby, A. Tahlawi, S. Brito dos Santos, A. Mantalaris, N. Panoskaltsis (corresponding)

title: A quantitative three-dimensional image analysis tool for maximal acquisition of spatial heterogeneity data
contribution: Image post-processing that uses analytic area corrections (2D) and validated Monte Carlo volume estimation (3D) to compute cell-density distributions over the whole confocal image, using about twice as many cells over far longer distances than centre-only methods.
problem_entry: 3D tissue imaging is costly and destructive, yet current analyses use only cells far from the image boundary, discarding nearly half of the data (pp. 4, 18).
key_idea: Concentric-shell densities with boundary-truncated areas computed analytically in 2D and by Monte Carlo in 3D, sampling within a small cuboid around each cell (9.1 min -> 22 s) (pp. 9, 13-14).
assumptions: Accuracy depends on user-defined bin widths and sample counts (p. 5); 10x lens as minimum magnification for single-cell recognition (p. 8).
proof_devices: Monte Carlo error measured against analytic 2D solutions over 4 geometries x 40 intervals to pick the convergence criterion (pp. 9-11)
synthetic uniform cell sets of known density recovered (p. 16)
with/without-void comparison on the same image (pp. 16-17)
experiments: Two stained bioreactor sections; 1116 vs 524 cells in a conservative comparison with current methods; manual scoring comparison (pp. 15-16).
positioning: Against centre-only analyses (Bjornsson et al.) and normalisation by random data; versus higher-resolution re-tiling approaches (pp. 18-19).
writing: Gains quantified as fold-changes in abstract and discussion (210% more cells, 23-fold distance, 50-fold range) (pp. 3, 18).
limits_future: Partition fineness vs boundary error trade-off with numbers (p. 18); extensions to MRI/CT and complex regions of interest (p. 20).

method_links.note: Step 5 analogue: the estimator is validated like an instrument against analytic solutions and synthetic known-density data before use on real images.
Comparison with current methods labelled conservative; accuracy targets set against controls.

transferable: Validate a Monte Carlo estimator on cases with closed-form answers, choose the convergence criterion from the error-vs-time curve, then apply it where no closed form exists (pp. 9-11).
Test the pipeline on synthetic data of known density with the real data's cell count and geometry (p. 16).
Restrict Monte Carlo sampling to a bounding box of known volume around each query (pp. 13-14).
coauthors: M. C. Allenby, N. Panoskaltsis, A. Mantalaris (corresponding)
